ECG-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Targeted Electrocardiogram Waveform Evolution

Abstract

Electrocardiogram (ECG) models need supervision that targets evolving weaknesses and remains faithful to waveform evidence. We introduce ECG-RSI, a recursive self-improvement framework combining verified waveform synthesis with feedback-guided intervention search. Signal remeasurement verifies waveform edits; construction errors guide generator repair, while learner errors motivate interventions compared on a separate selection set. Across seven benchmarks, three rounds raise Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's mean question-answering accuracy from 34.57% to 56.04% and mean classification F1 from 24.27 to 34.03. Across the retained trajectory, the preferred supervision shifts from direct reinforcement to confusion-focused contrasts. Continued feedback correction yields diminishing external gains. These results motivate separating error diagnosis from intervention selection and checking whether gains on the feedback set transfer to independent benchmarks.

1 Introduction

Electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation requires connecting waveform patterns to measurable features and clinically meaningful conclusions. Multimodal models have begun to learn this connection from ECG images and instruction data [30, 22, 18]. Effective ECG supervision grounds each answer in the waveform presented to the model. Changes in heart rate, intervals, or morphology can alter the interpretation of related ECG findings.

Existing studies improve ECG supervision through instruction construction and evidence-aware learning [30, 22, 18], while conditional signal generators expand waveform diversity [3, 20]. Yet it remains difficult to turn a learner’s specific weakness into a controlled training example. A generated waveform must express the intended ECG feature without introducing conflicting changes, and its question and answer must agree with the resulting signal. Training mixtures must adapt to newly identified weaknesses, persistent confusions, and shifts in task difficulty after each round. Our central insight is to use learner feedback to specify ECG evidence and signal measurements to verify it.

We propose ECG-RSI, a framework that connects targeted ECG data synthesis with feedback-driven recursive self-improvement (Fig. 1). Its data factory generates questions from existing signals and uses constrained reverse perturbations to synthesize waveforms with requested feature contrasts. The resulting waveforms are remeasured before their questions and answers are accepted. Construction failures guide revisions to perturbation operators and question-generation workflows, while the learner’s errors guide the categories, tasks, and difficulty levels of subsequent training data. At each round, candidate data recipes are used to train and compare model branches, and the selected branch informs the next round of synthesis and training.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We propose ECG-RSI, a framework that separates construction feedback for repairing data generation from learner feedback for proposing and comparing subsequent training interventions.

  • •

    We develop target-driven reverse waveform synthesis, which translates desired ECG feature contrasts into constrained signal perturbations and verifies the resulting waveforms to provide measurement-grounded supervision.

  • •

    We analyze how intervention utility changes with the learner: the retained trajectory shifts from direct reinforcement to confusion-focused contrasts, while continued feedback correction yields diminishing gains on external benchmarks.

2 Related Work

2.1 ECG Multimodal Learning and Evidence-Grounded Supervision

Medical vision-language foundation models provide a broader basis for domain adaptation. MedGemma adapts Gemma 3 models for medical image and text understanding and supports further task-specific fine-tuning [11]. Complementary work examines the integration of knowledge graphs with multimodal learning [6].

ECG-language models have progressed from ECG instruction tuning and multimodal alignment toward more flexible question answering and clinically grounded interpretation. PULSE, a multimodal large language model for ECG image comprehension, is instruction-tuned on ECGInstruct, an ECG image instruction dataset, and evaluated on ECGBench, a benchmark for ECG image interpretation [30]. GEM links signal and image representations to measurable ECG evidence [22]. ECG-R1 incorporates clinical protocols and diagnostic-evidence supervision into ECG interpretation [18]. Subsequent work broadens the types of questions, input formats, and supervision available to ECG models: anyECG-chat supports flexible ECG inputs and multiple tasks [25], Q-Heart introduces knowledge-informed ECG question answering [37], ECG-LLM uses clinically structured questions for cardiac reasoning [38], and ELF studies a simpler encoder-free ECG-language architecture [13]. MEETI aligns signals, images, extracted features, and interpretations within a multimodal ECG dataset [61], while ECG-Expert-QA provides diagnostically diverse questions for evaluation [44]. ECG input representations also affect performance [12]. Multi-source contrastive learning offers another way to broaden supervision: MS-ECG-FM aligns ECGs with ECG, echocardiography, radiology, and discharge reports, whose diagnostic information is complementary [24].

ECG Mirage probes whether predictions depend on the patient-specific ECG [26]. ECG-Reasoning-Benchmark examines stepwise ECG interpretation [36], and recent work evaluates ECG reasoning by separating waveform perception from clinical deduction [50]. Image-based model evaluations likewise expose the difficulty of reliable ECG interpretation from rendered tracings [42]. These studies motivate supervision that remains tied to the waveform presented to the learner. ECG-RSI addresses this need by constructing requested feature contrasts and deriving questions and answers from measurements of the resulting signals.

2.2 Conditional ECG Synthesis and Controlled Interventions

ECG synthesis has advanced through disease-conditioned adversarial generation [3], conditional diffusion [1, 41], clinical-text conditioning [8], and report- and patient-conditioned generation [20]. MIDT-ECG and FlowECG further investigate waveform fidelity, inter-lead coherence, and generation efficiency [16, 2]. More directly related to controllability, ECGTwin generates condition-guided personalized ECGs while seeking to preserve individual characteristics [21], and TransDiffECG explores semantically controllable signal generation [28]. Generative counterfactual ECGs have also been used to study how waveform changes affect an AI-ECG model’s predictions [17].

ECG-RSI constructs training examples for a specified learner weakness: it starts with a training-side waveform and a requested feature contrast, applies a constrained intervention, and remeasures the result. It accepts an example only when the intended change is achieved and relevant non-target properties are preserved; its question and answer are then grounded in the resulting waveform.

2.3 Feedback-Driven Data Evolution and Recursive Self-Improvement

Earlier self-improvement methods revise responses or retain verbal feedback [33, 39], generate instruction data [45, 49], or iteratively refresh reasoning supervision [58]. More recent systems connect generated tasks to learner improvement: CoEvolve guides task synthesis using learner behavior [54], NeoHorse-1 adapts post-training mixtures using capability evidence [35], and Absolute Zero and VisPlay couple task generation with solver improvement [64, 14]. SynCo makes this dependence explicit by jointly training a synthesizer and reasoner, with task validity, answer reliability, and outcome-grounded teachability providing feedback to the synthesizer [55]. Multiple reasoner rollouts per task provide this feedback, so estimated teaching value depends on the current policy’s observed outcomes. RSIBench-Data places data construction and selection at the center of RSI evaluation [34]. Related studies examine whether a self-synthetic pipeline continues to provide learnable information [32], while VISA revises multimodal instruction synthesis using verification and target-model failures [60]. Recursive on-policy distillation co-evolves the privileged teacher with the student [57], while RLTL;DR internalizes concise feedback from failed attempts [19]. Both make the supervision produced by an earlier attempt useful to subsequent learning.

A complementary line changes the mechanism of improvement: agent code and workflows [59, 62], skills [46], data preparation [53, 52], or environments and search strategies [65, 31]. These updates require assessment: revision selection [63, 48], evolving self-evaluation [29], hidden evaluations [43], and pairwise candidate ranking [10] provide different ways to compare candidates. Other studies guide subsequent adaptation [15, 5] or alternate harness evolution with model learning [51]. Structured knowledge is another object of improvement [7, 47]; in medicine, MedZERO couples task generation with evidence-grounded reasoning and controlled knowledge accumulation [9].

Paired evaluations also help identify diminishing returns and earlier artifacts worth retaining [56]. In a setting with frozen model weights, Agent Plasticity measures how efficiently experience produces future held-out gains relative to learning cost, showing that endpoint performance, acquisition efficiency, and transfer to harder conditions can diverge [40]. ECG-RSI grounds intervention proposals in ECG-specific error diagnostics: construction feedback repairs synthesis, learner feedback proposes interventions, and separate selection and external evaluations assess their utility.

3 Method

ECG-RSI couples verified synthesis with feedback-driven training (Fig. 1). Construction feedback checks waveform and question validity; learner feedback selects data for model-specific utility [34].

3.1 Framework and Feedback Interfaces

System state and data boundaries.

At round tt, the system state comprises the accepted learner θt\theta_{t}, retained training pool DtD_{t}, and construction policy ϕt\phi_{t}. The policy contains retrieval constraints, waveform operators, prompts, and reusable rules, separate from learner weights [59]. Source ECGs and morphology donors are restricted to training data and are patient-disjoint from development and independent evaluation data.

VfbV_{\mathrm{fb}} diagnoses errors; VselV_{\mathrm{sel}} selects models. Evaluation data are held out from generation and selection.

Two feedback loops.

Construction feedback identifies invalid waveform edits or questions and guides generator repair. Learner feedback guides recipes using gaps in ECG capability, question type, difficulty, and confusion pairs.

For a selected update path, one round can be summarized as

3.2 Targeted ECG Synthesis with Measurement-Grounded Supervision

3.2.1 Targeted Waveform Construction

Forward synthesis derives questions, answers, and explanations from measured training ECGs. Reverse synthesis edits an eligible waveform to express a requested feature contrast, then remeasures the signal before constructing supervision. Both routes check evidence, context, answer uniqueness, and explanation support.

Reverse requests come from learner weaknesses or distractors in training questions. A normal-versus-prolonged PR contrast specifies a measurable target and a corresponding waveform edit.

Target selection and constrained editing.

A delineator extracts u=f⁡(S)u=f(S) from ECG SS: heart rate (HR), R–R interval (RR), P-onset-to-QRS-onset interval (PR), QRS duration, QRS-onset-to-T-end interval (QT), corrected QT (QTc), and amplitudes. Feature kk on source ii is scored by si​k=ai​k​rk​dks_{ik}=a_{ik}r_{k}d_{k}: definability ai​ka_{ik}, reliability rkr_{k}, and diagnostic utility dkd_{k}. Eligible scores exceed the registered threshold. Appendix 7.6 details conversions, weighting, and scale normalization.

An eligible request specifies the target range, protected features and tolerances, permitted operators and donors, and attempt budget. The policy applies an operator sequence S′=Tδ​(S)S^{\prime}=T_{\delta}(S) after checking applicability. PR edits require P and QRS onsets; complex diagnoses require morphology beyond interval changes (Fig. 2).

3.2.2 Validation and Generator Repair

Re-extract u′=f⁡(S′)u^{\prime}=f(S^{\prime}) after editing. For target feature kk and requested change Δk\Delta_{k}, record the target error

Etarget=|[fk​(S′)−fk​(S)]−Δk|E_{\mathrm{target}}=\left|\bigl[f_{k}(S^{\prime})-f_{k}(S)\bigr]-\Delta_{k}\right|

separately from the drift of each protected feature jj,

Eprotect,j=|fj​(S′)−fj​(S)|.E_{\mathrm{protect},j}=\left|f_{j}(S^{\prime})-f_{j}(S)\right|.

Acceptance requires target and protected-feature errors to satisfy their respective tolerances, with checks of boundary continuity, unedited regions, lead consistency, morphology, leakage, diversity, and cost.

The accepted signal is rendered for question, answer, context, and explanation generation. Review requires a unique supported answer and evidence for each claimed observation, so supervision follows the remeasured signal.

Construction failure and generator repair.

Repairs follow failures [53]: signal errors guide operator revisions; missing morphology guides applicability/retrieval revisions; ambiguity guides question/context revisions; unsupported explanations guide prompt revisions.

Repairs record their trigger, changed rule, validation result, and scope. Old and revised versions are compared on matched sources, requests, seeds, and budgets; adoption requires signal and question checks to pass. Appendices 7.2 and 7.3 describe the rules and recording protocol; Appendix 10 provides stage prompts.

3.3 Feedback-Driven Recursive Model Improvement

3.3.1 Learner Diagnosis and Data Recipes

Errors, invalid outputs, and regressions guide recipes by category gg, learner-relative difficulty dd, and supervision ss:

πta​(g,d,s)=pta​(g)​pta​(d∣g)​pta​(s∣g,d).\pi_{t}^{a}(g,d,s)=p_{t}^{a}(g)\,p_{t}^{a}(d\mid g)\,p_{t}^{a}(s\mid g,d). (2)

Difficulty is learner-relative [64]. For training-side question ii, KiK_{i} independent answers under fixed decoding settings give p^i​t=Ki−1∑r=1Ki𝟏[y^i​r=yi]\widehat{p}_{it}=K_{i}^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^{K_{i}}\mathbf{1}[\widehat{y}_{ir}=y_{i}], used to group reliably solved, mixed-success, and unresolved examples. Probe budgets, scoring, output-validity requirements, and thresholds are fixed before branch comparison.

Supervision can retain the teacher explanation, expand intermediate ECG evidence, or add checks targeting an observed learner error. As in iterative reasoning supervision [58], explanations supply training targets; paired variants must preserve the verified image, question, options, answer, and clinical facts.

Recipes also fix source/edit constraints, replay, and training budgets. Recipe selection changes the data mixture; operator or prompt repair changes ϕt\phi_{t}. These interventions are tracked separately (Appendix 7.1).

3.3.2 Same-Parent Branch Exploration

Feedback and training-side probes define three recipe families from the same parent θt\theta_{t} [62, 65]:

  • •

    A: Direct reinforcement. Increase quotas for weak categories and question types while retaining related-category controls: a recipe for atrioventricular (AV) block emphasizes conduction measurements and diagnostic interpretation.

  • •

    B: Confusion contrast. Sample recurrently confused category pairs; construct options and explanations around their distinguishing ECG evidence. Regional ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) contrasts, for example, emphasize lead-specific localization.

  • •

    C: Difficulty and task curriculum. Reweight difficulty bins and question types using learner probes, e.g., increasing L3, multistep, or evidence-chain questions. Curriculum denotes a branch-specific mixture.

Recipes specify sampling quotas and construction requests: retrieve eligible waveforms or apply permitted edits, then run the shared measurement and question-validity gates (Section 3.2.2). Category, difficulty, and task constraints can overlap; Tab. 12 lists each round’s actual mixtures.

Each branch retains the same historical training manifest and adds 10,000 previously unused accepted questions, without an extra shared baseline set. All branches use three epochs of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with matched settings; the language model is updated while the vision encoder and multimodal aligner remain frozen. For ECG image II, question QQ, optional context CC, and explanation–answer target yy, the training loss is

ℒMCQ=−∑ℓlogpθ(yℓ∣I,Q,C,y<ℓ).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MCQ}}=-\sum_{\ell}\log p_{\theta}(y_{\ell}\mid I,Q,C,y_{<\ell}). (3)

Replay and new-data exposure are recorded in examples and tokens; training settings appear in Appendix 7.5.

3.3.3 Model Selection and Retained Lineage

After matched SFT, evaluate candidates on VselV_{\mathrm{sel}}. Apply the predesignated output-validity and non-target regression tolerances, then retain the highest-scoring qualifying checkpoint and its data [48]. Archive other branches; if none qualifies, retain the parent.

Reevaluate the retained learner on VfbV_{\mathrm{fb}} to construct new recipes: directions are reselected each round. Fig. 3 illustrates the process; Section 5.7 reports the choices.

4 Experiments

We evaluate benchmark performance, round-wise gains, and the training value of feedback-guided synthesis. The analysis asks how feedback granularity affects data utility, which candidate directions yield the strongest updates, and whether reductions in feedback errors transfer to external benchmarks.

The seven-benchmark aggregate (S7) is the equal-weight mean of four accuracy and three F1 scores on a 0–100 scale. MMMU-ECG, CSN, and G12EC use single-choice accuracy; ECG-QA uses exact-match accuracy over answer sets. PTB-XL, CPSC2018, and CODE-15% are multi-label classification tasks. F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall; Δ\Delta denotes an absolute score difference.

Evaluation tasks.

We evaluate eight ECG tasks comprising 10,840 items. The seven tasks included in S7 contain 10,697 items; the 143-item MedXpertQA-MM ECG subset is reported separately. S7 weights task scores equally and excludes MedX and LUDB. Appendix 8.5 (Tab. 19) lists the datasets, split identifiers, sample counts, and metrics.

4.1 Main Benchmark Results

Tab. 1 compares the recorded scores of closed-source, open-source, and ECG-specific models with ECG-RSI on seven benchmarks. ECG-RSI R3 has the highest S7 (46.61) among the compared models.

After three rounds, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's mean accuracy across the four question-answering (QA) benchmarks increases from 34.57% to 56.04%, a 21.47-percentage-point gain; its mean F1 across the three classification benchmarks increases from 24.27 to 34.03, a 9.77-point gain. Gains are calculated from unrounded means.

4.2 Evolution across Rounds

Tab. 2 and Fig. 4 show the R0–R3 trajectory of series R-A. Each winning branch adds 10,000 new accepted questions to the cumulative training set and replays all prior data. Appendix 8 provides feedback breakdowns.

Section 4.4 analyzes feedback errors by ECG capability, question type, and difficulty; Tab. 4 reports the question-type and difficulty breakdowns, and Tab. 5 reports the ECG-category breakdown.

4.3 Validation-Set Performance

MedX denotes the ECG subset of MedXpertQA. LUDB denotes the Lobachevsky University Electrocardiography Database, whose waveform annotations include P-wave, QRS-complex, and T-wave boundaries and peaks. The LUDB accuracy below refers to the ECG evaluation task constructed from that database.

Tab. 3 and Fig. 4(c) show that MedX accuracy rises from 51.57% to 57.24%, despite a small R2 decline. LUDB accuracy improves at every round, from 53.45% to 67.24%.

Fig. 4 summarizes round-wise benchmark and validation performance together with historical strategy trajectories.

5 Ablation Studies

We first assess waveform validity and the contribution of synthesis components. We then examine three linked questions: whether finer feedback improves training utility, whether the most prominent weakness determines the best training direction, and whether continued feedback improvement translates into external gains.

5.1 Effectiveness of the Synthesis Method

Quantitative waveform-feature validation.

We report waveform-feature error statistics, including mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE), from a single synthesis run of 10,000 samples in Tab. 6.

All six features meet the adopted MAE criteria (Status = Met), supporting numerical fidelity of the synthesized waveforms.

5.2 Blinded Review by Human Physicians

We randomly sample 240 examples stratified by six edit types (HR, RR, PR, QRS, QT, and QTc), with 40 examples per type. Two human physicians score the examples independently. We report 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the review metrics.

In stage 1, target labels, generation parameters, and teacher responses are hidden while waveform morphology and lead consistency are assessed. In stage 2, the physicians inspect the before/after waveforms and editing targets to assess target attainment and non-target preservation. Stage 3 assesses answers, explanations, and expected-parameter references.

Answer correctness and evidence support. Mean physician ratings are 0.88 for answer correctness and 0.76 for explanation support (κ=0.78\kappa=0.78). The stages assess morphology, editing fidelity, and answer/explanation quality.

Variation across edit types. Target attainment ranges from 0.78 for RR to 0.85 for HR. Explanation support varies from 0.72 to 0.78 and remains below answer accuracy for every edit type. The stratified results show that the gap is shared across editing targets.

The columns distinguish target attainment, preservation of non-target features, morphology consistency, answer accuracy, and explanation support.

5.3 Multi-Model Question-Quality Scores

Fig. 5 shows five-model scores across 23 ECG categories. R1 uses 10,000 of 16,193 candidate questions.

5.4 Data Construction and Feedback Selection

Four data configurations each add 10,000 SFT questions from the same checkpoint (S7 = 43.22).

Tab. 9 separates ordinary questions, forward synthesis, added reverse synthesis, and feedback-guided selection. Δ\DeltaS7 is relative to the shared checkpoint. Ordinary questions and forward-only synthesis yield similar scores (44.15 and 44.27). Adding reverse synthesis raises S7 to 45.56; feedback-guided selection further raises it to 46.23, the largest gain.

5.5 Synthesis-Component Ablation

Tab. 10 compares synthesis updates at a fixed target of 10,000 accepted questions. The full method requires 16,193 candidates to reach this target, versus 36,723 with operator updates frozen and 22,398 with skill updates frozen (2.27 and 1.38 times as many, respectively). Freezing updates reduces question-quality scores and downstream R1 S7.

5.6 Feedback Granularity and Training Utility

To isolate feedback resolution, Tab. 11 compares four selection configurations from the same parent (S7 = 43.22), each adding 10,000 accepted questions. Only the feedback dimensions used for selection vary.

The fixed-mixture and four-dimensional configurations share their endpoints with Tab. 9. Category-only feedback yields S7 = 45.60, close to 45.56 with fixed selection. Adding question type raises S7 to 45.98; including difficulty and confusion pairs raises it further to 46.23. With the same added-data volume, resolving these finer capability gaps produces more useful training examples.

5.7 Round-Wise Branch Selection and Data Composition

Feedback-guided branch evolution compares candidate interventions at each round and retains the best qualifying update on a separate selection set. Tab. 12 reports all three same-parent candidates at each transition. Each candidate adds 10,000 accepted questions with matched historical replay and training settings. Selection uses SselS_{\mathrm{sel}} on VselV_{\mathrm{sel}}, distinct from external S7.

From weak-category coverage to discriminative evidence.

Direct reinforcement is preferred in the first comparison, despite a 52% Mobitz I/II confusion error in the parent. Branch A reaches Ssel=42.66S_{\mathrm{sel}}=42.66, compared with 40.51 for the contrast-focused branch. Its emphasis on AV-block coverage and measurement is followed by reductions in L3 and Mobitz II errors (Tab. 13). A prominent confusion therefore does not, by itself, identify the best candidate intervention in this comparison.

The later comparisons favor confusion-focused supervision. Regional STEMI contrasts score 45.08 in R1→\toR2, versus 44.12 for direct reinforcement and 43.55 for curriculum adjustment. Rhythm contrasts score 46.03 in R2→\toR3, versus 45.90 and 44.71 for the alternatives. L3 errors remain substantial throughout these comparisons, but the curriculum-focused candidate is not selected in either comparison.

Tab. 13 connects the selected recipes to subsequent feedback outcomes. Both later recipes retain 4,500 L3 questions while changing the targeted diagnostic contrasts, illustrating that difficulty and content are overlapping recipe choices.

5.8 Comparison of RSI Evolution Strategies

Tab. 14 and 15 compare tree, uniform-allocation, and chain trajectories in R-A. Tree finishes at S7 = 46.61, ahead of uniform (41.45), chain (43.70), and chain's best round (44.75).

All three strategies improve over R0. In the final round, tree rises from 46.23 to 46.61, while uniform falls from 43.25 to 41.45 and chain from 44.75 to 43.70. Chain leads R1; tree finishes highest.

5.9 Results Analysis

Fine-grained feedback improves training utility.

With a shared parent and 10,000 added questions, S7 reaches 46.23 with full feedback, versus 45.56 with fixed selection and 45.60 with category-only feedback (Tab. 11).

Error diagnosis proposes candidates; comparison selects the update.

The retained path in Tab. 12 changes from direct reinforcement to confusion-focused supervision. This supports treating feedback as a source of candidate interventions, rather than a deterministic prescription for the next data mixture. The training utility of a proposal is assessed by comparing candidates from the same parent.

Useful training evidence changes with the learner.

The selected data move from AV-block measurements to regional STEMI contrasts and then rhythm contrasts. These changes concern both what evidence is targeted and how it is presented. Historical data are replayed, while fresh feedback redirects the next additions; the reported path therefore reflects repeated intervention selection rather than repetition of a fixed recipe.

Local correction has diminishing external returns.

In the category-level summary, feedback error falls from 39.63% to 21.33% across R0–R3, but successive external S7 gains shrink to 13.07, 3.01, and 0.38 (Tabs. 8.2 and 2). ECG-QA, CPSC2018, and CODE-15% regress in R3 despite fewer feedback errors. In this run, continued correction on the feedback set is therefore insufficient to characterize external progress. Transfer value and regressions must be examined alongside error frequency.

6 Conclusion

ECG-RSI combines verified bidirectional synthesis with empirical comparison of training interventions. The retained recipe shifts from direct reinforcement to confusion-focused contrasts as the learner changes. This supports separating weakness diagnosis from intervention selection within the tested setting: an error profile proposes directions, while candidate comparison determines which update to retain.

Across three rounds, S7 rises from 30.15 to 46.61, and MedXpert ECG accuracy from 51.57% to 57.24%. Operator and skill updates improve synthesis efficiency and downstream performance. However, continued feedback-error reductions yield diminishing S7 gains, so transfer and regression checks remain necessary for interpreting progress beyond the feedback set.

Declaration of AI Assistance.

AI tools assisted with language polishing, formatting, and figure preparation.

Reproducibility Statement.

The main text reports benchmark trajectories, feedback diagnostics, controlled ablations, blinded clinical review, and model-based question-quality scores. Supplementary materials provide the construction and training protocols, category-level records, prompts, and complete case responses. The present release is limited to the manuscript; the implementation and training-data files are not released.

7 Supplementary Method Details

7.1 Student-Conditioned Data Recipes

Equation (2) defines the joint recipe over category, difficulty, and supervision representation.

Here gg is a task/capability category, dd is learner-relative difficulty, and ss is a supervision representation. Each recipe also registers retrieval/edit constraints, replay, and budgets. The operator and prompt library ϕ\phi determines which requests can be constructed. Selecting among fixed templates changes the recipe; editing a template or operator changes the library version. These interventions must be evaluated separately.

Difficulty estimation.

With the current learner and decoding settings fixed, answer each training-side candidate independently KiK_{i} times and estimate difficulty from its fraction of correct responses:

p^i​t=1Ki∑r=1Ki𝟏[y^i​r=yi].\widehat{p}_{it}=\frac{1}{K_{i}}\sum_{r=1}^{K_{i}}\mathbf{1}[\widehat{y}_{ir}=y_{i}]. (5)

Group candidates into reliably solved, mixed-success, and unresolved questions.

Supervision representations.

A verified question can have (i) the original teacher rationale, (ii) an evidence-expanded rationale making required intermediate observations explicit, and (iii) an error-targeted rationale adding checks motivated by the student’s observed failure pattern. “Chain of thought (CoT)” denotes teacher-generated explanations used for supervision. Store token count under the student’s tokenizer, required evidence-step coverage, and the checks added. Paired expansions preserve the image, question, options, answer, and clinical facts.

Difficulty belongs to the current learner.

Register the rollout budget, concept-level scoring, position-counterbalancing policy, minimum valid-output rate, and binning thresholds before branch comparison. Approximate bins are reliably solved, mixed success, and unresolved; 0/Ki0/K_{i} denotes unresolved performance under this probe. Parsing/truncation remain separate flags: report end-to-end correctness and correctness conditional on valid output.

ECG-specific supervision repair.

For a QRS-width error, a candidate expanded target identifies QRS onset/offset, converts grid distance to milliseconds, and checks the threshold, using independently verified fiducials. If measurements are already correct but the label is wrong, add the relevant cross-lead differential evidence. Error type and waveform evidence guide interventions, supported by contrastive probes, scored outputs, and signals.

Fig. 3 maps feedback to data-selection and generation requests for branch validation.

7.2 Construction Feedback and Versioned Repair

Acceptance also checks leakage and diversity.

Repair by failure type.

Acceptance tracks target attainment, non-target drift, continuity, lead consistency, morphology, context, answer uniqueness, and cost. Target errors or boundary artifacts guide operator revisions; missing morphology guides applicability/retrieval revisions; ambiguity guides question/context revisions; unsupported explanations guide prompt revisions.

Reusable rules and version records.

Each skill specifies applicability, sources, operator order, parameter ranges, failure handling, and question rules. Updates record feedback, changes, proposer, both versions, validation results, and next-round scope. Compare the original and revised versions on the same source signals, requests, random seeds, and attempt budgets, and adopt revisions after independent operator and question regression checks.

7.3 Waveform Construction and Validation Details

Bidirectional synthesis and reverse perturbation.

The forward route measures and renders a real training waveform, then constructs a supported question, context, and answer. The reverse route selects an eligible training waveform for a target contrast, applies constrained operators, and remeasures it before rendering and question construction.

A PR-interval contrast requires measurable P and QRS onsets. The edit must reach the target range while preserving heart rate and QRS morphology within fixed tolerances. Complex disease patterns require verified morphology and clinical evidence. Both routes share question, context, and explanation checks. Bidirectional synthesis creates examples; dual feedback repairs construction and chooses subsequent requests.

Sources: (i) retrieved training ECGs, (ii) reused/reweighted accepted questions, (iii) training-distractor targets, (iv) controlled edits, and (v) audited training-side morphology donors. Check feasibility, applicability, and evidence.

For a source SS and permitted donor set, construct S′=Tδ​(S)S^{\prime}=T_{\delta}(S) and re-extract u′=f⁡(S′)u^{\prime}=f(S^{\prime}). Store target error |[fk​(S′)−fk​(S)]−Δkrequest||[f_{k}(S^{\prime})-f_{k}(S)]-\Delta_{k}^{\mathrm{request}}| and protected drift |fj​(S′)−fj​(S)||f_{j}(S^{\prime})-f_{j}(S)| separately. Check continuity, unedited regions, lead alignment, and class morphology. Sources/donors are patient-disjoint from feedback, selection, and evaluation.

7.4 Bounded Recipe Search within the Learning Loop

Construction feedback validates examples and guides generator repair. Learner feedback supplies the demand profile and delayed utility for recipe selection. Each round follows five registered steps:

  1. 1.

    Score the accepted learner on VfbV_{\mathrm{fb}} and probe training candidates to update category, difficulty, and error profiles.

  2. 2.

    Propose a bounded recipe set 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t} from these profiles and prior outcomes; save the proposer and exact recipe.

  3. 3.

    Construct and validate each recipe’s training data under fixed gates. From the same parent checkpoint, run matched small-budget SFT branches with fixed replay and optimizer settings.

  4. 4.

    Compare candidates under the registered selection protocol, including forgetting and output validity.

  5. 5.

    Promote the accepted candidate and its recipe/policy versions, then remeasure for the next round. Full-budget retraining of a pilot winner restarts from the registered parent and requires validation before promotion.

For branch aa, the simplest candidate utility is

Δ​Ut​(a)=Ssel​(SFT⁡(θt,Dta∪Rt,b))−Ssel​(θt),\Delta U_{t}(a)=S_{\mathrm{sel}}\!\left(\operatorname{SFT}(\theta_{t},D_{t}^{a}\cup R_{t};b)\right)-S_{\mathrm{sel}}(\theta_{t}), (6)

Here Δ​Ut​(a)\Delta U_{t}(a) is the selection-score improvement of branch aa over its parent, not a weighted sum over branches. SselS_{\mathrm{sel}} evaluates a learner on VselV_{\mathrm{sel}} and is distinct from the external seven-benchmark score S7. Here bb is the shared pilot budget; SselS_{\mathrm{sel}} is the preregistered capability-macro score over fixed eligible tasks.

Each round trains candidate branches from the same parent, compares them on a fixed development set, and retains the best qualifying branch. The next round starts from that model, while unselected branches are archived. The search tree records candidates; the retained path records the selected model updates.

Fig. 3 illustrates candidate exploration and checkpoint inheritance, with a colored example lineage. Section 3.3.2 defines the three recipe families; Tab. 12 reports measured compositions, scores, and selections.

7.5 Training Configuration

Each round uses three training epochs and a maximum sequence length of 28,672 tokens. Packing, padding-free batching, and sequence parallelism are enabled. The micro-batch size is per GPU.

Parameter Setting Parameter Setting
Sequence and topology Optimization
Epochs / maximum tokens 3 / 28,672 Optimizer Distributed Adam
Micro-batch / global batch 1 / 32 Peak / minimum LR 10−510^{-5} / 10−710^{-7}
Gradient accumulation 1 Schedule / warmup Cosine / 5%
GPUs (nodes ×\times GPUs) 128​(16×8)128\ (16\times 8) Weight decay / grad. clip 0.1 (constant) / 1.0
DP / TP / PP / CP 32 / 4 / 1 / 1 Adam β1/β2/ϵ\beta_{1}/\beta_{2}/\epsilon 0.9/0.95/10−80.9/0.95/10^{-8}
EP / ETP 8 / 1 Compute / master precision bfloat16 / float32
Packing / padding-free Enabled / enabled CPU offload fraction 1.0
Modules and experts
Attention backend FlashAttention Grouped GEMM Enabled
Recompute modules core_attn, moe, mlp Permutation fusion Disabled
Shared-expert overlap Enabled Auxiliary loss / router dtype 10−610^{-6} / float32

DP, TP, PP, CP, EP, and ETP denote data, tensor, pipeline, context, expert, and expert-tensor parallelism.

Distributed Adam uses cosine learning-rate (LR) decay with 5% warmup. Computation uses bfloat16; master parameters, gradients, and Adam states use float32. Optimizer CPU offload is enabled with fraction 1.0.

The language model is trainable; the vision encoder and multimodal aligner are frozen. Selected modules are recomputed, with FlashAttention as the attention backend. GEMM denotes general matrix multiplication.

Open-data curation and capacity-aware post-training for broader multimodal reasoning are also studied in MMVistaReason [27].

7.6 Parameter Extraction and Selection Details

A delineator supplies candidate measurements

u=f⁡(S),u∈ℝM.u=f(S),\quad u\in\mathbb{R}^{M}. (7)

At 25 mm/s, a 1 mm horizontal square is 40 ms and a 5 mm square is 200 ms; at 10 mm/mV, 1 mm vertically is 0.1 mV (a 5 mm square is 0.5 mV). PR is measured from P onset to QRS onset, and QT from QRS onset to T offset.

The parameter selector uses reliability and diagnostic utility,

rk=1/σ^k∑j1/σ^j,r_{k}=\frac{1/\hat{\sigma}_{k}}{\sum_{j}1/\hat{\sigma}_{j}}, (8)
si​k=ai​k​rk​dk,s_{ik}=a_{ik}r_{k}d_{k}, (9)
𝒞i={k:si​k>τparam}.\mathcal{C}_{i}=\{k:s_{ik}>\tau_{\mathrm{param}}\}. (10)

Here ai​ka_{ik} is definability, σ^k\hat{\sigma}_{k} an extraction-error scale, and dkd_{k} a probe-based utility.

Scale specification. Comparing inverse error scales across features requires a common dimensionless normalization, with reference scales for measurements in bpm, ms, and mV.

8.5 Evaluation Splits

MMMU-ECG is the MMMU-inspired ECG multiple-choice task in ECGBench. CSN denotes Chapman–Shaoxing–Ningbo; G12EC denotes the Georgia 12-Lead ECG Challenge Database. ECG-QA (ECG-QA: A Comprehensive Question Answering Dataset Combined With Electrocardiogram) uses questions based on PTB-XL. CPSC2018 denotes the China Physiological Signal Challenge 2018, and CODE-15% is the public subset of Clinical Outcomes in Digital Electrocardiography. MedXpert-ECG contains ECG questions selected from MedXpertQA-MM. The configurations ptb-test-report (500 items) and arena (50 items) are not enabled and are excluded from the total. LUDB is evaluated separately from these eight splits.

Figure labels MMMU, G12, ECGQA, PTB, CPSC, and CODE15 correspond to MMMU-ECG, G12EC, ECG-QA, PTB-XL, CPSC2018, and CODE-15%, respectively.

11.1 Case 1: PR prolongation

Case 1 error analysis. At 25 mm/s, 130 ms corresponds to 3.25 small boxes, not the 2.6 stated in one part of the response. Bundle branch block assessment combines QRS duration with characteristic morphology. The response also references the intended answer and calibrates estimates from option values.

11.2 Case 2: Heart-rate slowing

Case 2 error analysis. Eight beats in ten seconds give approximately 48 bpm. Seven R–R intervals span the first to last R peaks. The response justifies QRS duration by the synthetic origin and invokes the intended answer.
